title: GOSWAMI v MOTO KARE LIMITED (IN LIQUIDATION) and Ors

DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY
Employment Relationship Problem
[1] Suraj Goswami commenced employment with Moto Kare Limited (MKL) on 14 June
2023. Mr Goswami was employed in the position of car groomer and detailer.

[2] Mr Goswami signed an individual employment agreement with MKL. Mansha Chopra
is the director of MKL. Jagmeet Singh is married to Ms Chopra. Mr Goswami says Mr Singh
exercised significant control over the administration and management of MKL.
[3] On 26 March 2026, MKL was placed into liquidation by the court.
[4] Although MKL has been placed into liquidation, if the Authority is satisfied that there
has been a default in the payment of money by MKL due to a breach of employment standards,
it may consider the potential liability of individuals pursuant to s 142Y of the Employment
Relations Act 2000 (the Act).1
[5] In his application to the Authority, Mr Goswami seeks:
(a) wage arrears in the sum of $39,440.69;
(b) payment for public holidays in the sum of $5,234.63; and
(c) payment of outstanding annual holiday pay in the sum of $7,717.11.
[6] Mr Goswami says MKL breached the terms of his individual employment agreement
by not paying him the correct contractual rate, not paying for all hours worked, and not
providing 40 hours of work each week.
[7] Mr Goswami says Ms Chopra and Mr Singh aided and abetted these breaches of his
individual employment agreement. Therefore, Mr Goswami seeks penalties against Ms Chopra
and Mr Singh.2
[8] Mr Goswami maintains MKL breached s 4 of the Wages Protection Act 1983 (WPA)
by not paying wages when they became payable. He also says MKL breached s 27 of the
Holidays Act 2003 (HA03) by not paying outstanding annual holiday pay and public holiday
payments, s 130 of the Act by not providing his wages and time record upon request, and s 82
of the HA03 by not providing access of his holiday and leave record upon request.
1 Lawton v Steel Pencil Holdings Limited (in liquidation) [2021] NZEmpC 199 at [37].
2 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 134(2).

[9] Therefore, Mr Goswami seeks penalties for breaches of these statutory provisions.
[10] Mr Goswami says Ms Chopra and Mr Singh were persons involved in breaches of
employment standards and seeks leave of the Authority to recover wages or other money
payable to the extent MKL is unable to pay the arrears of wages or other money, pursuant to s
142Y(2) of the Act.
The Authority’s investigation
[11] Ms Chopra lodged a statement in reply on behalf of the respondents. On Thursday 21
May 2026 a case management conference (CMC) was held to progress Mr Goswami’s
application.
[12] At the commencement of the CMC the Authority attempted to contact the respondents
but was unsuccessful. The respondents did not attend the CMC. The CMC continued in the
absence of the respondents. The respondents were provided with a fair opportunity to participate
in the CMC.
[13] The Authority served the directions and notice of investigation meeting in accordance
with the regulations.3
[14] At the scheduled start time the respondents were not in attendance at the investigation
meeting. At my direction, the investigation meeting commenced after the advised start time to
accommodate possible lateness on the part of the respondents. The respondents did not attend
the investigation meeting.
[15] For the Authority’s investigation, a written witness statement was lodged by
Mr Goswami.
[16] As permitted by s 174E of the Employment Relations Act 2000 (the Act) this
determination has stated findings of fact and law, expressed conclusions on issues necessary to
dispose of the matter and specified orders made. It has not recorded all evidence and
submissions received.
3 Employment Relations Authority Regulations 2000, reg 16.

[20] According to the agreement Mr Goswami was guaranteed, and required to work, 40
hours per week. The business operated between the hours of Monday to Sunday, 8am to 7pm.
Mr Goswami was to be paid $29.70, according to the agreement.
[21] MKL has not supplied the Authority with Mr Goswami’s wages and time record.
[22] Mr Goswami’s ability to bring an accurate claim pursuant to s 131 of the Act, has been
prejudiced by MKL’s failure to produce a wages and time record.4
[23] I now consider the evidence provided by Mr Goswami in support of his claim for wage
arrears.5
[24] Mr Goswami kept contemporaneous records of his working hours using the notes
application on his mobile phone.
[25] Mr Goswami provided the Authority with WhatsApp messages. Some of these
WhatsApp messages, between Mr Singh and Mr Goswami, include details about days and hours
worked by Mr Goswami.
[26] Some of the WhatsApp messages refer to “23”, being the dollar amount MKL paid
Mr Goswami for hours worked.
[27] This means, at least on some occasions, Mr Goswami was paid materially less than the
contracted hourly rate of $29.70 per hour.
[28] In some of the WhatsApp messages, Mr Goswami asks MKL to pay his wages so he
can meet his personal financial obligations.
[29] In the individual employment agreement, MKL guaranteed Mr Goswami 40 hours of
work per week. However, relying on bank statements, WhatsApp messages and
contemporaneous records of hours worked, Mr Goswami has explained to the Authority that he
was frequently not offered 40 hours of work.
4 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 132(1).
5 Employment Relations Act 2000, s 132(2).

[30] Mr Goswami’s work visa was issued on the basis that he would be employed by MKL
as a full-time permanent employee working 40 hours per week.
[31] Based on the evidence provided by Mr Goswami to the Authority, I accept as proved all
claims he has made in respect of wages he was paid, and the hours, days and times he worked
for MKL.6
Did MKL breach s 4 of the WPA?
[32] Mr Goswami has provided evidence to the Authority which establishes there were
instances when MKL did not pay wages owed to Mr Goswami at the time they became payable.
[33] As recorded earlier in my determination, MKL frequently did not pay wages when they
fell due and did not pay Mr Goswami the correct contractual rate.
[34] Therefore, MKL breached s 4 of the WPA, which is also a breach of an employment
standard.7
Did MKL breach Mr Goswami’s individual employment agreement?
[35] Based on the findings I have made with reference to the express term in Mr Goswami’s
individual employment agreement, requiring MKL to offer him 40 hours of work per week, and
the requirement to pay Mr Goswami $29.70 per hour, I am satisfied that MKL breached clause
7.2 (hours of work) and clause 8.1 (hourly rate).
Should a penalty be issued against Ms Chopra and/or Mr Singh?
[36] Mr Goswami says that Ms Chopra and Mr Singh aided and abetted the breaches of his
individual employment agreement.
[37] Although Ms Chopra is the director of MKL, it is clear from the evidence given by

Did MKL breach employment standards?
[53] The definition of employment standards is set out in s 5 of the Act, and includes the
provisions of the WPA, minimum entitlements and payment for those under the HA03, and the
requirements of sections 81 and 82 of the HA03.14
[54] Based on the findings set out in this determination, I am satisfied that MKL breached
the following employment standards:
(a) section 4 of the WPA;
(b) minimum entitlement provisions pursuant to the HA03; and
(c) the requirements of sections 81 and 82 of the HA03.
Were Ms Chopra and/or Mr Singh persons involved in breaches of employment
standards?
[55] According to s 142W of the Act, a person is “involved in a breach” if the breach is a
breach of an employment standard and the persons has aided, abetted, counselled, or procured
the breach.
[56] As recorded earlier in my determination, although Ms Chopra is the director of MKL,
it is clear from the evidence given by Mr Goswami, evidence in the form of WhatsApp
communications, and in Mr Goswami’s submissions, that Mr Singh directed Mr Goswami’s
work, managed the business and managed the payroll.
[57] At the investigation meeting, Mr Goswami said he met Ms Chopra on “two or three
occasions”.
[58] The knowledge required to establish liability for a person “involved in a breach” of
employment standards under s 142W(1) of the Act is knowledge of the essential facts that
establish the contravention by the employee.15
14 Employment Relations Act, s 5.
15 A Labour Inspector v Southern Taxis Limited [2021] NZCA 705 at [59].

[59] I find that Mr Singh was a person involved in the breaches of employment standards.
Mr Singh knew that Mr Goswami was not being paid according to the contractual rate,
WhatsApp messages confirm that Mr Singh was asked by Mr Goswami for payment of his
wages because wage payments were not accurate and not paid on time, and Mr Singh managed
the payroll for MKL.
[60] By order of the court, MKL was placed into liquidation. According to the first
liquidators report, the sum of $950,582 is owed by MKL to unsecured creditors.
[61] I find that MKL is unable to pay the sums owed, arising from the breaches of
employment standards to Mr Goswami.
Summary and orders
[62] I grant leave to Mr Goswami to recover the following sums of money from Mr Singh:
(a) wage arrears in the sum of $39,440.69;
(b) payment for public holidays in the sum of $5,234.63; and
(c) payment of outstanding annual holiday pay in the sum of $7,717,11.
[63] Within 28 days of the date of this determination, I order Mr Singh to make the following
payments to Mr Goswami:
(a) $3,000 in respect of a penalty, pursuant to s 134(2) of the Act.
(b) $39,440.69 (gross) for wage arrears.
(c) $5,234.63 (gross) for public holidays owing.
(d) $7,717.11 (gross) for annual holiday pay owing.
Costs
[64] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between
themselves.
[65] If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is
